title: Pushing Against a Candidates Flaw
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece recommends a specific interview technique for handling a strong candidate who displays one glaring flaw: confront it directly rather than quietly passing on them. It provides an example script for raising a perception of arrogance directly with a candidate, framing the conversation as diagnostic rather than accusatory. The resulting exchange reveals whether the candidate is self-aware and reflective or defensive and in denial, which itself provides valuable signal. The article frames this as a low-cost, high-value step that also does the candidate a service by giving them rare, honest feedback.
points: A single glaring flaw shouldn't automatically disqualify an otherwise strong candidate.
The recommended move is to confront the flaw directly with the candidate rather than quietly passing.
How a candidate responds to the confrontation — self-aware versus defensive — is itself valuable signal.
The exercise gives candidates rare, direct feedback about why they were perceived negatively.
The article frames this as low-cost with little downside beyond mild discomfort.
quotes: Occasionally, a job candidate with huge upside displays a glaring flaw that prohibits their selection.
But before giving up on a promising candidate with a fatal flaw, it would be wise to first push against the blemish and see what the team can learn.
The ensuing conversation will expose how self-aware the candidate is, why they engaged the team leader in that way, and what they typically do to offset such a defect.
Candidates who are in denial of the perceptions others form or get defensive about how they presented themselves confirm that they are not a good fit.
Teams that make their thinking explicit with candidates act as leaders, offering hugely valuable feedback to someone who clearly needs it.
